docs.text: IBM Bob Level 3 i. What is IBM Bob? IBM Bob is an AI-powered partner for the entire software development lifecycle (SDLC) , and it lives where your developers already work: inside the development environment itself. It is tempting to file Bob alongside the many code-completion assistants that have flooded the marketplace since LLMs arrived — but that comparison sells it short. Bob is not simply a code generator, but a partner for every step in your weekly workflow (for both developers and sellers, alike.) A code generator helps at the single moment a function gets written. Bob is built to help across the whole arc of a project: planning a feature before a line of code exists, reasoning about an unfamiliar codebase, implementing changes, and automating the repetitive work that surrounds real development. A word on working with generative AI IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most developers are accustomed to. In practice, that means the same prompt can produce different code from one run to the next. This is both a strength and a quirk of the technology, and it is something to work with rather than against. Precision is what tips the odds in your favor. The more clearly you describe what you want, the more closely Bob's output will mirror your intent; conversely, the smallest change in wording can meaningfully change the generated code. Throughout this lab, your results may differ from the solutions shown — and that is expected, not a defect. Whenever an output diverges, you have three good options: refine the prompt and try again, edit the generated code by hand, or simply proceed if the variation still compiles and runs. Human review remains essential at every step, and never more so than while you are still learning the tool. And At its core, Bob does three things exceptionally well: Writes and modifies code across an entire codebase, from natural language instructions Understands codebases — reading and reasoning about complex project structures, dependencies, and architectural patterns Automates the busywork of development, from documentation to commit messages to test scaffolding ii. Bob across the software development lifecycle The distinction worth holding onto is scope . Where a traditional assistant is anchored to the moment of writing or fixing code, Bob is designed to support the lifecycle around it — helping you plan features before implementation begins, understand the full context of a project before making changes, and keep the developer in control at every step. Bob augments the way your teams already work; it does not replace their judgment. Hold on to that last idea, because it is the thread that runs through everything in this course. iii. Where Bob meets you: the IDE and the Shell Bob comes in two form factors, so it can meet developers wherever they are most productive: Interface Description Bob IDE A VS Code extension providing an agentic sidebar, inline code assistance, and mode-based interaction Bob Shell A terminal-based interface offering the same capabilities in a keyboard-driven, automation-friendly form You will spend most of this course in the Bob IDE, where the visuals make each capability easy to see. In the final module we will step over to Bob Shell — and you will find that everything you have learned carries over. iv. The journey ahead: the AI-assisted code maturity curve Most product tours are really just feature inventories — a parade of buttons and panels with no story tying them together. This course is organized differently. The four modules ahead trace the AI-assisted code maturity curve — and as you shift right along it, you hand Bob progressively more responsibility, with Bob earning that trust by keeping you in command the entire way. Module Stage What it means for your developers — and your clients 1 Assist Bob accelerates everyday work in the editor, and you accept or reject every change. Velocity from day one, at near-zero risk. 2 Delegate Bob takes a whole feature from idea to working code — but builds only what you reviewed and approved first. 3 Tailor Bob learns your codebase, enforces your standards, and adapts to each role, so it behaves like a teammate who already knows how you work. 4 Scale & Extend Bob stays reliable on large, long-running work and plugs into the tools your enterprise already runs. Notice the single idea that recurs at every stage: the developer stays in control. What changes is only the stakes. At the Assist stage, control means accepting each suggestion keystroke by keystroke. At Delegate , it means approving the plan before a line is written. At Tailor , it means encoding the very rules Bob must obey. At Scale & Extend , it means governing context, credentials, and tool access. Same promise; rising trust. That escalation is the story — and it is the story your sellers can carry into a C-suite conversation: not "here are some features," but "here is how your teams grow into an AI partner without ever losing the wheel." v. The world we'll build in: Galaxium Travels Watch first: Chapter 1: Demo Application: Galaxium Travels [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) walks through the demo scenario that ties the hands-on modules together. [2 min] Every good demonstration needs a believable world to unfold in, and ours is Galaxium Travels — a fictional luxury space-travel booking system whose source code is publicly available on GitHub. Rather than show Bob against throwaway snippets, we will work against this single, production-style codebase from start to finish. It is the consistent backdrop against which each stage of the curve comes to life. Galaxium Travels follows a familiar full-stack shape: Frontend: React and TypeScript Backend: Python, exposing both REST and MCP interfaces Database: SQLite, with seed data for development and testing The backend is organized around a SQLite database containing the domain's data models (flights, users, bookings), the schemas that validate them, and seed data to work with. It exposes the application two ways: a REST API of standard HTTP endpoints for the frontend and other clients, and an MCP interface — a Model Context Protocol interface that lets Bob interact with the backend directly, as a tool. A local API browser is also available, so you can exercise endpoints (retrieving flights, registering users, making bookings) without the frontend in the way. The React/TypeScript frontend, for its part, connects to those same REST endpoints and presents the experience an end user would see: browsing available flights, registering and signing in, and booking a seat. As you move through the course, you will add real features to this application — and the order is deliberate, because each builds on the last: Email validation — Module 1.1, Next Edit Prediction Retry logic for API calls — Module 1.2, Literate Coding Seat-class tiers (Economy, Business, Galaxium) — Module 2, the Agentic Sidebar Working in one continuous codebase is the point: it lets you watch Bob operate the way it would inside a client's real project, not in the tidy isolation of a toy example. The full source is on GitHub if you would like to explore it independently. Module 1 — ASSIST · Bob in Your Flow This is the first stage of the curve, and the gentlest. Here, Bob works shoulder to shoulder with the developer inside the editor — anticipating the next keystroke, drafting the next few lines, making targeted edits on request — while the developer accepts or rejects every single change. The value to pitch here is immediate and low-risk: your teams move faster without breaking their train of thought, and nothing lands in the codebase that they did not explicitly choose. It is the most natural possible on-ramp to working with an AI partner, and it pays off from the very first session. 1.1 — Staying in Flow: Tab Completion & Next Edit Prediction Watch first: Chapter 2.1: Next Edit Prediction and Tab Completion [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) demonstrates Bob's tab completion and next edit predictions. [1 min] Why this matters The quickest way to lose a developer's confidence in an AI tool is to pull them out of their flow. Bob's first two capabilities are designed to do the opposite — to keep a developer in the work while quietly removing friction from it. They are tab completion and next edit prediction , and they operate as a pair: the first suggests code from context, the second anticipates where you will need to go next. How tab completion works Tab completion is a familiar idea executed unusually well. Where conventional autocomplete reacts to the few characters you have just typed, Bob reads the surrounding context to make a genuinely informed suggestion — drawing on the comments describing your intent, the patterns and structure already present in the code, your project's conventions and style, and related code in other files. The result feels less like word-completion and more like a colleague finishing your thought. Accepting suggestions When Bob offers a suggestion, you stay in charge of it: Press Tab to accept it Keep typing to override it Watch it update dynamically as you continue Next edit prediction Real code changes are rarely confined to one spot. Add a field, and you often need to use it elsewhere; introduce a function, and something downstream has to call it. Next edit prediction is built around that reality: after you accept a suggestion, Bob anticipates the related edit you are likely to need and moves you there. The rhythm is simple — describe what you want in a comment, let Bob suggest the code, press Tab to accept, and press Tab again to jump to the next predicted location, where Bob positions your cursor exactly where the new code needs to be used. Expect some variation. Generative AI is non-deterministic, so your results may differ from what you see here. If an output diverges, refine the prompt, follow up with another, or adjust the code by hand — or simply carry on if what you have works. Hands-on: adding email validation with Next Edit Prediction Follow the video for a full walkthrough of this scenario: Chapter 2.1: Next Edit Prediction and Tab Completion [IBM Bob L3] A reminder before you start: because you are working with generative AI, your results may not match the screenshots exactly — and that is perfectly fine. Better still, most hiccups can be resolved without touching a line of code yourself. If you notice a discrepancy between this guide and what you see on screen, describe it to Bob in plain language; more often than not, it will sort the problem out for you. Let's give Galaxium Travels a feature it is currently missing — validation of the email addresses users type when they sign in. In the VS Code activity bar, click Explorer (Ctrl+Shift+E) . Click Open Folder . The File Explorer window opens... In your File Explorer view, highlight the galaxium-travels folder and select the folder. Our galaxium-travels folder appears. The file we'll work on for Module 1.1 is UserIdentification.tsx . Navigate to it at: \ booking_system_frontend > src > components > user > UserIdentification.tsx Now, we see UserIdentification.tsx has been opened. Navigate under the UserIdentification function (this should be around line 19 in UserIdentification.tsx) Navigate under the UserIdentification function (this should be around line 19-21 in UserIdentification.tsx), and type: //validate email addresses Then add a blank line before and after this commented line. With //validate email addresses in place, press Enter , then Tab . When Tab Completion is working, you will see this greyed-out text. If nothing appears , simply repeat the process: return to the commented line, press Enter , and press Tab again. Press Tab once more, and the greyed-out suggestion is committed to your file as working code. Because Bob's suggestions are non-deterministic, your generated function may look quite different from the one shown here. Even if the result is unexpected, you can keep going as long as your code runs. If the generated code does not compile, first compare the inserted function with the example shown in the lab, then either correct the function manually or delete the generated code and repeat the prediction step. If necessary, use the Agentic Sidebar to diagnose the error. In this run, Next Edit Prediction took a different route — rather than offering the whole function at once, it suggested the code line by line.\ \ Press Tab when each suggestion appears. Another single-line suggestion appears. Press Tab to accept it. A return statement appears; press Tab once more to accept it. With that return statement, the function is complete. Bob happened to reach for a regular expression (regex) here, much as a developer might — but your version may differ, or take an entirely different approach. That is expected and entirely acceptable; the only test that matters is whether your code runs. Now let's return to the Galaxium Travels web app and confirm the change took effect. To do so, we will need to reboot our web app. Return to your already-open terminal window — the one running Vite — and open a new terminal there by pressing the Plus icon. Next, close the other Terminal windows. Depending on your operating system, upon closing the tabs you may receive a pop-up message saying that you will terminate a process. This is expected; and it's okay to proceed with closing the window. MAC AND LINUX ONLY \ \ With all the previously-running Terminal windows closed, we are now ready to reload the app. On macOS or Linux, run the following commands one at a time: cd ~/galaxium-travels ./start.sh\ \ You should see "Galaxium Travels is running!" (amongst the other success messages) once the app starts running. Proceed to Step 22 (move to opening the web app on your browser, skip the Windows parts) WINDOWS ONLY \ \ On Windows, first, execute the following commands. Send them one-by-one, all in the same terminal window.\ \ These are the same manual backend startup steps as per the Registration Guide, but without the step of installing requirements.txt. cd $HOME\galaxium-travels cd booking_system_backend python -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\activate python server.py WINDOWS ONLY Upon executing all of these commands, open a new Terminal window by pressing the Plus button ( do not close the current Terminal window ). WINDOWS ONLY In the new Terminal window, next, execute the following commands. Send them one-by-one, all in the same terminal window. cd $HOME\galaxium-travels cd booking_system_frontend npm run dev Open your web browser and return to the Galaxium Travels site by typing the following in your search bar: \ http://localhost:5173/ \ and pressing Enter. You're back on the Galaxium Travels site. Click Flights . Click Book Now under any of the listed flights. Clicking Book Now opens a Sign In window. Now let's confirm your email-validation logic is doing its job. Put any text that would be improperly formatted email address in the Email field - for instance, a random sequence of symbols like: $$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$ Notice that you can't proceed — that string of dollar signs is plainly not a valid email address. So what happens if we add an @ symbol? Still rejected — symbols like $$$$$$$$ aren't permitted in a domain name. The function you generated with Next Edit Prediction may lead to different behaviour. 1.2 — Editing by Intent: Literate Coding Watch first: Chapter 2.2: Literate Coding [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) demonstrates Bob's literate coding capabilities. [2 min] Why this matters Tab completion and next edit prediction shine while you are writing new code. But much of a developer's day is spent making a precise, deliberate change to code that already exists — and for that, literate coding is the tool. It lets you write a natural-language instruction directly inside a file, exactly where the change belongs, much as you would jot a comment. Bob reads the instruction in place and produces a targeted, localized modification. The developer is still describing intent in plain language; the difference is that here you are pointing at a specific spot and saying "change this ." Entering literate coding mode You enter literate coding through the magic wand icon in the VS Code editor. Once active, it lets you: Write natural-language instructions at a precise code location Target the exact section you want changed Place several instructions, at several locations, within a single file How it works The workflow is deliberately simple: Position your cursor where the change belongs Click the magic wand icon to enter literate coding mode Type a natural-language instruction describing the change you want For changes that span several places, add an instruction line at each one Click Generate to produce the modifications The diff view: change with full visibility This is where the control in the Assist stage becomes tangible. Bob never silently rewrites your file. Instead, it presents every change in a diff view that shows the added code, the removed code, and enough surrounding context to understand the scope of what is changing. You review, then you decide. Nothing is committed until you say so. Where literate coding shines Literate coding is at its best for focused, in-place work: Wrapping logic around existing code — retry mechanisms, error handling, or logging Refactoring a specific block while leaving the surrounding logic untouched Quick, targeted modifications to a single function without disturbing the broader structure For sweeping, multi-file changes or architectural restructuring, you will reach for Code mode instead — which is exactly where Module 2 picks up. A note on this scenario. Generative AI is non-deterministic, so your results may vary. If an output differs, refine the prompt or adjust the code — or proceed if what you have works. Hands-on: adding retry logic with Literate Coding Follow the video for a full walkthrough: Chapter 2.2: Literate Coding [IBM Bob L3] Galaxium's backend can be slow to respond when fetching flight information, and occasional timeouts are the result. It is a perfect candidate for a small, surgical fix: we will use literate coding to wrap the flight-fetching call in retry logic — without hand-writing any of it. Back in the IDE, open Flights.tsx \ \ (booking_system_frontend > src > pages > Flights.tsx) Click the magic wand icon near the top of the editor — or press Ctrl + I — to activate literate coding mode. A bar appears at the bottom-center of the screen with two arrows, Clear All , and Generate — you are now in literate coding mode! On line 43 in Flights.tsx, type: the backend is unreliable at times. We need a retry logic here The text should highlight to show the mode is active. Treat the visible mode state and the Generate button as your primary indicators, since the exact highlight color can vary by release. Unlike tab completion, there is no need to comment this instruction out. With the instruction written, press the Generate button. A diff view appears. Removed code is shown in red, and added code in whatever highlight your build uses for additions (yellow in this capture; some versions use green). Review the on-screen diff carefully before accepting. If everything looks right, press Accept All . The red lines are removed, and the new highlighted lines are written into the file. This particular change may not produce anything visible in the running app — and that is by design; the point is to watch targeted code generation happen in context , against real code. Take a moment to read what Bob produced, and then we will move on. Key takeaways Literate coding turns a plain-language instruction, written in place, into a precise code change. The diff view keeps you in full control — you see every change before it lands. It is most powerful for focused, single-file modifications. For multi-file or architectural changes, Code mode is the right tool — and that is where we go next. These are not optional viewing. They show — on screen and in real time — exactly how each feature behaves, a level of detail that text alone struggles to convey. This is expected; and it's okay to proceed with closing the window. MAC AND LINUX ONLY \ \ With all the previously-running Terminal windows closed, we are now ready to reload the app. On macOS or Linux, run the following commands one at a time: cd ~/galaxium-travels ./start.sh\ \ You should see "Galaxium Travels is running!" (amongst the other success messages) once the app starts running. Proceed to Step 22 (move to opening the web app on your browser, skip the Windows parts) WINDOWS ONLY \ \ On Windows, first, execute the following commands. Send them one-by-one, all in the same terminal window.\ \ These are the same manual backend startup steps as per the Registration Guide, but without the step of installing requirements.txt. cd $HOME\galaxium-travels cd booking_system_backend python -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\activate python server.py WINDOWS ONLY Upon executing all of these commands, open a new Terminal window by pressing the Plus button ( do not close the current Terminal window ). WINDOWS ONLY In the new Terminal window, next, execute the following commands. Send them one-by-one, all in the same terminal window. cd $HOME\galaxium-travels cd booking_system_frontend npm run dev Open your web browser and return to the Galaxium Travels site by typing the following in your search bar: \ http://localhost:5173/ \ and pressing Enter. You're back on the Galaxium Travels site. Click Flights . Click Book Now under any of the listed flights. Clicking Book Now opens a Sign In window. Now let's confirm your email-validation logic is doing its job. Put any text that would be improperly formatted email address in the Email field - for instance, a random sequence of symbols like: $$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$ Notice that you can't proceed — that string of dollar signs is plainly not a valid email address. So what happens if we add an @ symbol? Still rejected — symbols like $$$$$$$$ aren't permitted in a domain name. The function you generated with Next Edit Prediction may lead to different behaviour.

docs.text: Watch first: Chapter 2.2: Literate Coding [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) demonstrates Bob's literate coding capabilities. [2 min]
docs.title: 1.2 — Editing by Intent: Literate Coding

docs.text: Tab completion and next edit prediction shine while you are writing new code. But much of a developer's day is spent making a precise, deliberate change to code that already exists — and for that, literate coding is the tool. It lets you write a natural-language instruction directly inside a file, exactly where the change belongs, much as you would jot a comment. Bob reads the instruction in place and produces a targeted, localized modification. The developer is still describing intent in plain language; the difference is that here you are pointing at a specific spot and saying "change this ."
docs.title: Why this matters

docs.text: You enter literate coding through the magic wand icon in the VS Code editor. Once active, it lets you: Write natural-language instructions at a precise code location Target the exact section you want changed Place several instructions, at several locations, within a single file
docs.title: Entering literate coding mode

docs.text: The workflow is deliberately simple: Position your cursor where the change belongs Click the magic wand icon to enter literate coding mode Type a natural-language instruction describing the change you want For changes that span several places, add an instruction line at each one Click Generate to produce the modifications
docs.title: How it works

docs.text: This is where the control in the Assist stage becomes tangible. Bob never silently rewrites your file. Instead, it presents every change in a diff view that shows the added code, the removed code, and enough surrounding context to understand the scope of what is changing. You review, then you decide. Nothing is committed until you say so.
docs.title: The diff view: change with full visibility

docs.text: Literate coding is at its best for focused, in-place work: Wrapping logic around existing code — retry mechanisms, error handling, or logging Refactoring a specific block while leaving the surrounding logic untouched Quick, targeted modifications to a single function without disturbing the broader structure For sweeping, multi-file changes or architectural restructuring, you will reach for Code mode instead — which is exactly where Module 2 picks up. A note on this scenario. Generative AI is non-deterministic, so your results may vary. If an output differs, refine the prompt or adjust the code — or proceed if what you have works.
docs.title: Where literate coding shines

docs.text: Follow the video for a full walkthrough: Chapter 2.2: Literate Coding [IBM Bob L3] Galaxium's backend can be slow to respond when fetching flight information, and occasional timeouts are the result. It is a perfect candidate for a small, surgical fix: we will use literate coding to wrap the flight-fetching call in retry logic — without hand-writing any of it. Back in the IDE, open Flights.tsx \ \ (booking_system_frontend > src > pages > Flights.tsx) Click the magic wand icon near the top of the editor — or press Ctrl + I — to activate literate coding mode. A bar appears at the bottom-center of the screen with two arrows, Clear All , and Generate — you are now in literate coding mode! On line 43 in Flights.tsx, type: the backend is unreliable at times. We need a retry logic here The text should highlight to show the mode is active. Treat the visible mode state and the Generate button as your primary indicators, since the exact highlight color can vary by release. Unlike tab completion, there is no need to comment this instruction out. With the instruction written, press the Generate button. A diff view appears. Removed code is shown in red, and added code in whatever highlight your build uses for additions (yellow in this capture; some versions use green). Review the on-screen diff carefully before accepting. If everything looks right, press Accept All . The red lines are removed, and the new highlighted lines are written into the file. This particular change may not produce anything visible in the running app — and that is by design; the point is to watch targeted code generation happen in context , against real code. Take a moment to read what Bob produced, and then we will move on.
docs.title: Hands-on: adding retry logic with Literate Coding

docs.text: Literate coding turns a plain-language instruction, written in place, into a precise code change. The diff view keeps you in full control — you see every change before it lands. It is most powerful for focused, single-file modifications. For multi-file or architectural changes, Code mode is the right tool — and that is where we go next.

docs.title: **i.

docs.text: IBM Bob is an AI-powered software development lifecycle (SDLC) partner that integrates directly into the development environment. Bob operates across the full development lifecycle — not just as a code generator, but as a partner that supports planning, implementation, and automation throughout a project. Bob's core capabilities: Code writing and modification : Writes new code and modifies existing code across the entire codebase based on natural language instructions Codebase understanding : Reads and reasons about complex project structures, dependencies, and architectural patterns Development task automation : Automates repetitive tasks such as documentation, commit message generation, and test scaffolding
docs.title: What is IBM Bob?

docs.text: The distinction between Bob and a traditional code generator is scope. Bob is designed to support the entire software development lifecycle, not just the moment of writing a function or fixing a bug. This includes: Helping plan features before implementation begins Understanding the full context of a project before making changes Keeping the developer in control at every step Bob augments existing workflows rather than replacing developer judgment.
docs.title: Bob as an SDLC Partner

docs.text: Bob is available in two primary form factors: Interface Description Bob IDE VS Code extension providing an agentic sidebar, inline code assistance, and mode-based interaction Bob Shell Terminal-based interface offering the same capabilities in a keyboard-driven, automation-friendly form factor
docs.title: Interfaces

docs.text: This learning path covers IBM Bob across five chapters: Chapter Focus 1 Demo setup and environment introduction 2 Core interaction patterns: tab completion, next edit prediction, and the agentic chat 3 Customization: project context, custom rules, and custom modes 4 Advanced topics: context window management and Bob Shell 5 Extending Bob's capabilities with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) Each chapter builds on the previous, progressing from basic interactions to advanced configuration and integration.
docs.title: Learning Path Structure

docs.text: Bob supports the full software development lifecycle, not just code generation Two interfaces are available: Bob IDE (VS Code) and Bob Shell (terminal) The developer remains in control — Bob assists with reasoning and implementation, but does not replace developer judgment This learning path progresses from beginner to advanced topics across five chapters
